name: Battle of Isandlwana
info: A Zulu army of some 20,000 overran part of the British main column at Isandlwana in Zululand on 22 January 1879, early in the Anglo-Zulu War, killing over 1,300 troops and bringing a larger second British invasion.

facts.place: The British camp below the hill of Isandlwana in Zululand, in what is now South Africa, some 11 km from the valley where the Zulu army was found
facts.sides: The British Empire under Lord Chelmsford, with Colonel Henry Pulleine commanding the camp and Colonel Anthony Durnford leading a part of it: approximately 1,800 British, colonial and native troops with approximately 350 civilians, of whom over 1,300 troops were left in the camp. The Zulu Kingdom under King Cetshwayo, with the army commanded by Ntshingwayo kaMahole and Mavumengwana kaNdlela Ntuli: some 20,000 warriors
facts.outcome: A Zulu victory. Over 1,300 troops of the British force were killed, including Pulleine and Durnford, and the first British invasion of Zululand collapsed. Zulu dead are put at 1,000 to 3,000 in all.

t: A Zulu army of some 20,000 armed mainly with spears and cowhide shields overran about 1,300 British and colonial troops with modern rifles, after Lord Chelmsford had divided his force and left the camp unentrenched.
Estimates of Zulu dead run from 1,000 to 3,000, since neither the British nor the Zulu counted them; of the British force, over 1,300 were killed.
The defeat made the British government commit to a heavily reinforced second invasion and ended King Cetshwayo's hopes of a negotiated peace.
dyk: A solar eclipse fell at 2:30 pm on the day of the battle, and a Zulu warrior recalled that the sun turned black in the middle of the fighting and then came out bright again.
ev: The High Commissioner Sir Henry Bartle Frere gives King Cetshwayo an ultimatum that he could not possibly meet
Lord Chelmsford's centre column crosses the Buffalo River into Zululand when the ultimatum has expired
The Zulu army leaves Ulundi, and the British pitch camp at Isandlwana without entrenching
Chelmsford leaves the camp with about 2,800 soldiers to find the Zulu army, and the Zulu army attacks the camp in his absence
About 4,000 Zulu reserves cross the Buffalo River and attack the mission station at Rorke's Drift, but are repelled
A reinforced British army invades Zululand again under Chelmsford, with Sir Garnet Wolseley sent to replace him
Disraeli's government falls, Bartle Frere is recalled and the policy of Confederation is abandoned

sections.background:
It was thought in Britain that a plan like the one that had brought about the Confederation of Canada in 1867 might succeed in South Africa, and in 1877 Sir Henry Bartle Frere was appointed High Commissioner for Southern Africa to carry it out. Two obstacles were the South African Republic and the Kingdom of Zululand, both of which the British Empire would try to overcome by force. On his own initiative, without the approval of the British government and intending to bring on a war with the Zulu, Frere gave the Zulu king Cetshwayo an ultimatum on 11 December 1878 that the king could not possibly meet.

When it expired a month later, Frere ordered Lord Chelmsford, commander of British forces, to invade, for which plans had already been made. Chelmsford at first planned five columns of over 17,000 troops, meant to encircle the Zulu army and force it to fight, since he feared it would avoid battle and strike at Natal. He settled on three columns, the centre column of over 8,500 men under his own direction. It consisted of No. 3 Column under Colonel Richard Thomas Glyn and Colonel Anthony Durnford's No. 2 Column. Early on 11 January the centre column began crossing the Buffalo River into Zululand. The invasion began in the rainy season, which slowed the British advance to a crawl.

The Zulu army was essentially a militia that could stay in the field only a few weeks. The British had timed the invasion to catch the warrior-farmers dispersed at harvest, but the army had already begun to assemble at Ulundi for the First Fruits ceremony.
sections.forces:
The backbone of Chelmsford's force was twelve regular companies, six each of the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the 24th Regiment of Foot, regarded as hardened and reliable. There were about 2,500 African auxiliaries of the Natal Native Contingent, many of them exiled or refugee Zulu, led by European officers and generally thought poor by the British, since they were barred from their own way of fighting, ill trained in the European one and indifferently armed. The troops had the Martini-Henry breechloading rifle, two 7-pounder mountain guns and a Hale rocket battery.

The Zulu army carried assegai thrusting spears, known as iklwa, knobkierrie clubs and cowhide shields, and drilled in their use. A few warriors had old muskets and antiquated rifles, but marksmanship was poor, powder and shot were of dreadful quality and many warriors held firearms to be the arms of a coward. The army of some 20,000 was commanded by Ntshingwayo kaMahole and Mavumengwana kaNdlela Ntuli. Its listed right horn was 3,000 to 4,000, the chest 7,000 to 9,000, the left horn 5,000 to 6,000 and the reserve 4,000 to 5,000.

Chelmsford pitched camp at Isandlwana on 20 January but did not follow standing orders to entrench and formed no laager, saying it would take a week to make. On 22 January he left at dawn with approximately 2,800 soldiers, about half the British infantry and around 600 auxiliaries, to find the Zulu force. He left over 1,300 men under Brevet Lieutenant Colonel Henry Pulleine: about 600 of the 24th, around 700 others and about 70 Royal Artillery gunners with two guns.
sections.course:
Pulleine, an administrator without front-line experience, received reports from early morning of Zulu groups, the first at 7:00 am. Around 10:30 am Colonel Durnford arrived from Rorke's Drift with 500 men of the Natal Native Contingent and a rocket battery. He was senior but did not overrule Pulleine's dispositions, and after lunch he moved out to engage a Zulu force that both officers judged to be moving against Chelmsford's rear. Around 11:00 am scouts under Lieutenant Charles Raw chased some Zulus into a valley and saw most of the 20,000 sitting in silence. The Zulu army, discovered, advanced at once, and fell into its 'horns and chest of the buffalo' formation as it ran.

Pulleine put all six companies of the 24th into an extended firing line. Durnford's men met the Zulu centre and fell back to a donga on the British right, where many of the native troops began to leave. For an hour or so until after noon British volleys and shell fire pinned down the Zulu centre and stalled its advance, while the left horn moved to envelop the British right. The Zulu tell of an older warrior who exposed himself to fire to urge the others on before the line broke. As Durnford's men withdrew, the regulars' right flank was exposed and Pulleine ordered a withdrawal to the camp, which the 24th made in good order. G Company, 2nd/24th, was overrun quickly.

The eclipse came at 2:30 pm. In the camp the fighting was hand to hand and no quarter was given to the British wounded. The killing ran back along the Fugitive's Drift. Lieutenant Melvill carried a colour off on horseback and lost it crossing the river; he and Lieutenant Coghill were killed.
sections.aftermath:
Of the 1,800-plus British troops and African auxiliaries, over 1,300 were killed, most of them Europeans, including Pulleine and Durnford. Only five Imperial officers survived, and of 52 officers lost, 21 were of the 24th Foot. The Natal Native Contingent lost some 400 men, and 240 of 249 amaChunu auxiliaries were killed. Captured Natal Native Contingent soldiers were regarded as traitors by the Zulu and executed. Some officers in dark patrol dress were spared because the Zulu had been told to ignore civilians in black coats. Over 1,000 rifles, two guns, four rocket troughs, 400,000 rounds, three colours and 130 wagons were taken or left on the field.

Neither side counted the Zulu dead. Ron Lock and Peter Quantrill put them at perhaps 1,500 to 2,000, Ian Knight at at least 1,000 killed outright, and Mike Snook at 1,500 to 2,000 dead with a similar number wounded. Cetshwayo is quoted as saying that an assegai had been thrust into the belly of the nation.

Chelmsford learned of the fall of the camp about 3:30 pm and reached it at sundown, after the Zulu had left. Near the end of the fighting about 4,000 reserve warriors crossed the Buffalo and attacked Rorke's Drift, which some 150 British soldiers held. The Zulu made no other attempt to cross into Natal, which Cetshwayo had forbidden. Natal's towns nonetheless made laagers. The British government, wanting to avenge the defeat, to avoid losing the next election and to show the Empire was not vulnerable, committed itself to a reinforced second invasion.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from British survivors and officers, Zulu accounts and the ground itself. Horace Smith-Dorrien, one of the survivors, gave the view that the British were slow to unpack ammunition boxes. An officer ahead of Chelmsford's force watched the end of the fight from a distance, and a Zulu warrior described the eclipse. A Zulu account describes a group of the 24th forming a square on the neck of Isandlwana. The Horse Guards interrogation of August 1879, under the Duke of Cambridge, concluded that the primary cause of the defeat was an under-estimate of the Zulu army's offensive power. Many bodies were found in large groups, now marked by cairns, including one stand of around 150 men, which suggests the resistance lasted longer than once thought.

Much is disputed. The valley where the Zulu army was found is generally thought to be the Ngwebeni, some 11 km from the camp, but may have been closer, near the spurs of Nqutu hill. Lock and Quantrill argue that the diversions that drew more than half of Chelmsford's force away were deliberate and that the Zulu were not discovered by chance but were deployed and ready to advance. Donald Morris argued that the men ran out of ammunition, while Knight and Snook hold that most of the firing line did not, although Durnford's men probably did, and Knight concludes that the British were defending too large a perimeter. The story of a lone soldier of the 24th who held a cave until late afternoon is considered by modern historians historically unconfirmed and partly romanticised.
sections.legacy:
The British Army had suffered its worst defeat against an indigenous foe armed with vastly inferior technology. In none of the other engagements of the war did the British again fight the main Zulu army in their typical line, the Thin Red Line, in open field. They entrenched or formed very close order, such as the square, and ammunition boxes were thereafter unscrewed in advance. Chelmsford blamed Durnford for the defeat, although there is no evidence that he had ordered a proper camp to be made; Garnet Wolseley wrote that the blame was thrown on Durnford to screen Chelmsford.

After the second invasion, Chelmsford defeated the Zulu in several engagements, the last at Ulundi, and Cetshwayo was captured. Some historians hold that Ulundi was a token victory, driven by his need to salvage some success. Bartle Frere was recalled in August 1880 and the policy of Confederation was abandoned. By the time Cetshwayo was allowed to return home, the Zulu Kingdom had ceased to exist as an independent entity.

Melvill and Coghill received posthumous Victoria Crosses in 1907, after long campaigning by Mrs Melvill, and Wolseley had objected to the idea of officers escaping on horseback while their men on foot were killed. The legend of the lone soldier in the cave inspired Richard Thomas Moynan's 1883 painting The Last of the 24th. The battle is the subject of Johnny Clegg and Juluka's song Impi, the 1979 film Zulu Dawn and the opening scene of the 1964 film Zulu.

summary: At Isandlwana on 22 January 1879 a Zulu army of some 20,000 overran the British camp left behind by Lord Chelmsford, killing over 1,300 troops. The Zulu dead are put at 1,000 to 3,000. It was the British Army's worst defeat by an indigenous foe and brought a second, larger invasion.
notes: The article's account of its own sources is thin; the sources section is built from the named witnesses and historians it cites.

Zulu strength: the lead says some 20,000; the Prelude says Cetshwayo sent a 24,000-strong main impi, then 4,000 detached, leaving 20,000. Order-of-battle ranges sum to 19,000 to 24,000. I used 20,000.

British numbers: the lead says approximately 1,800 troops with approximately 350 civilians; the Prelude says 1,300 left in camp, over 1,300 killed 'of the 1,800-plus'. The Prelude also gives 4,700 men in No. 3 Column and over 3,800 in No. 2 Column, which do not match these; not used.
The article gives 'around 600' auxiliaries leaving with Chelmsford beside 2,800 soldiers 'including half of the British infantry'; used as written. Chelmsford says 'over 4,000' in his reasoning.
The article spells the Zulu commander Ntshingwayo and Ntshigwayo; the Zulu army's wings in the order of battle list 'Loins (Reserves)' which I called the reserve.

The article gives the camp's rocket battery as two 9-pr troughs (Durnford's) and 'four rocket troughs' captured; left as the article has it in the aftermath. A 2025 publication claim about N/5 Battery's rocket troughs was left out.
The valley: the article says 7 miles (11 km) from the camp, 'but may have been closer'. In the facts I wrote 'some 11 km' for the Ngwebeni distance as given.

Garbled or odd: 'The article's sentence 'There was no casualty count ... since they abandoned the field' is muddled about who abandoned the field; left out. 'Zulu Prince Ndanbuko' and the commander kaNthati appear once; left out. Survivors 'most were from the auxiliaries' left out. The Man in the Cave paragraph is partly in an informal register and mentions 'C Company (Captain Reginald Younghusband)' while the Prelude says only G/2nd and five companies of the 1st are present; I kept only the unconfirmed-story point.
Ulundi: the article gives no date, so the event list says 1879 only for the second invasion generally.

Left out: the Isandlwana description of Pulleine moving the firing line 'about 20 minutes' in; the 'Irishman guarding Chelmsford's tent' story; Wolseley's statement on the Prince Imperial; Hamilton-Browne's message and Harness's and Black's return; the Zulu's missed opportunity after the battle; the surgeon-major Peter Shepherd; Gabangaye's death.
